title: Lost in the sands, found in the genes: the systematic placement and ecology of the unique Central Asian winter moth Cheimoptena pennigera Danilevsky, 1969 (Lepidoptera: Geometridae)
content:
Abstract
The systematic placement of the enigmatic monotypic geometrid genus Cheimoptena Danilevsky, 1969 has long been contentious. We used a multi-locus approach, analysing eight molecular markers (COI, GAPDH, RpS5, wingless, EF-1α, ArgK, Ca-ATPase, and H3) to clarify its phylogenetic position. Preliminary analysis revealed an error in the GenBank database: a COI barcode identical to Cheimoptena pennigera was found in the published mitogenome of the saturniid Neoris haraldi, suggesting the species’ presence in northwestern China. Subsequent reconstructions with comprehensive taxonomic sampling consistently placed Cheimoptena within a strongly supported clade comprising the tribes Campaeini, Alsophilini, and Prosopolophini. Although Cheimoptena is firmly nested within this complex, it is difficult to assign it to a specific tribe due to topological instability across trees. We addressed the potential impact of long-branch attraction, concluding that the clustering of Cheimoptena with this tribal complex is robustly driven by a genuine phylogenetic signal rather than methodological artefacts, while internal branching remains sensitive to outgroup selection. In terms of morphology, Cheimoptena exhibits a mosaic of characters, sharing similarities in genital structures with Alsophilini and pupal features with Prosopolophini. We confirm Cheimoptena represents an isolated, early-diverging lineage within this complex and maintain its status as a distinct tribe, Cheimoptenini.
